title: Design Detectability and a Ceiling Effect in a Preregistered Verifier‑in‑the‑Loop NL→Config Evaluation
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired confirmatory evaluation (N=200 paired multi‑device intents) that measured the marginal benefit of a bounded generate–validate–repair pipeline placing a formal verifier (Batfish) in‑the‑loop versus a single‑pass LLM generation for natural‑language→configuration translation. The preregistered design produced a single shared initial LLM candidate per intent that served as the starting point for both baseline and guarded arms. In the confirmatory cohort this shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator in every paired episode: baseline_success_count = 200, guarded_success_count = 200, repair_attempts = 0/200, paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0 (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0 and the preregistered 95% bootstrap percentile CI is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). Because the shared‑candidate pairing required the guarded branch to change that single candidate to create discordant pairs, the preregistered primary paired test is uninformative for assessing marginal repair utility under these generation semantics. We (1) document the deterministic validator decision rule used to assign verifier_pass, (2) present artifact‑grounded counts and representative diagnostics that substantiate the observed ceiling effect, (3) analyze the detectability tradeoff that produced a formal power collapse under the preregistered assumptions, and (4) provide concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future preregistered NetOps evaluations to restore sensitivity to marginal verifier utility.

sections.introduction: Generative language models are increasingly proposed as components of NetOps toolchains that translate operator intent into device configurations and automated workflows. A common mitigation pattern for unsafe or hallucinated outputs is to place a formal network verifier in a generate–validate–repair loop so that verifier counterexamples drive constrained repairs before device execution. Quantifying the marginal benefit of such guarded pipelines—relative to single‑pass LLM generation—matters for operational adoption because it informs tradeoffs among latency, complexity, and safety. We preregistered study CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 to answer the confirmatory question: To what extent does an iterative generate–validate–repair loop using a formal verifier (Batfish) reduce critical semantic errors in LLM‑generated multi‑device configurations when evaluated in an emulation‑grounded closed loop? The preregistration fixed a paired design (N=200 paired intents), a single shared initial generation per intent (shared_initial_candidate), and at most one verifier‑guided repair iteration. The run completed as preregistered but produced a design‑induced ceiling effect: the shared initial candidate already satisfied the deterministic validator for every paired episode. This left the preregistered paired test blind to potential marginal repair utility. The contribution of this paper is methodological: we provide an artifact‑grounded account of the ceiling effect, a formal explanation of the detectability tradeoff induced by shared‑candidate pairing, representative diagnostics from the archived run, and concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations to avoid such detectability collapse in future preregistered NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: Recent literature on LLMs for NetOps spans intent translation, configuration synthesis, programmatic repair, and agentic orchestration; surveys and architecture proposals repeatedly recommend verifier integration as a practical mitigation for hallucination and semantic errors. Executable benchmark efforts and closed‑loop testbeds demonstrate that verifiers (e.g., Batfish, Header‑Space based tools) can detect reachability and policy violations and, in several studies, improve syntactic/executable correctness of generated configs. At the same time, prior work highlights a gap between interface/linguistic tasks and procedural/execution tasks—the so‑called execution wall—and calls for richer, trace‑centered evaluation methodologies that include tool calls and provenance. Our study builds on these bodies by providing a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment and by showing a concrete experimental design failure mode (detectability collapse) that can arise when generation semantics are traded for within‑pair variance control. The empirical artifacts we reference and compare to prior proposals and benchmarks are listed in the cited record set and include executable benchmark proposals and verification‑tool literature that motivated the present design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 preregistered the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and specified a two‑sided exact McNemar test (alpha = 0.05) plus a 95% bootstrap percentile CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000). The confirmatory sampling plan fixed N = 200 paired multi‑device intents stratified into three topology clusters: (A) 2 devices: 80 intents; (B) 3–4 devices: 80 intents; (C) 5–8 devices: 40 intents. The preregistration, task generator, sampling seed (42), and exclusion rules were archived prior to execution.

Generation semantics and orchestration. The run used a single shared_initial_candidate generation per intent: the pipeline generated one LLM candidate (shared) and supplied that identical candidate as the starting response for both the baseline and the guarded conditions. The intent of shared_initial_candidate was to reduce between‑intent generation variance and isolate any effect of the verifier‑guided repair step. The declared model for the run was gpt‑5‑mini and the execution configuration is archived in execution/model_configuration.json (the run used provider traces recorded under execution/). The maximum model_calls and repair budget were enforced per the preregistration (maximum_model_calls = 400, maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The execution adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the emulation stack used containerized Mininet‑style networks with FRRouting and VyOS images.

Deterministic validator and pass rule. We implemented deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the scorer that maps an LLM candidate to a binary verifier_pass outcome. The validator_trace archived for each candidate contains validation_before and validation_after records. The validator assigns verifier_pass only when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0. Operationally this corresponds to three sequential checks applied to each candidate: (1) parsing/command canonicalization and syntactic executability checks; (2) task‑payload constraint enforcement (required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state invariants); and (3) Batfish reachability/policy checks executed on the emulated topology where Batfish counterexamples are translated to violation codes. The validator_trace structure and representative scorer outputs are archived under execution/scoring/*.json and per‑task scoring artifacts (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json).

Timeouts, missingness, and contamination controls. Timeouts and retry policies followed the preregistration: LLM call timeout = 60s with one immediate retry, Batfish verification timeout = 120s, and emulation timeout = 300s per intent. Exact‑hash duplicate detection and n‑gram overlap flags were computed during sampling; exact‑hash duplicates were excluded from the confirmatory sample (none were found), and high n‑gram‑overlap flags were recorded for sensitivity reporting (none flagged in confirmatory N). All raw responses, provider traces, validator traces, and logs were archived for machine verification (execution/, analysis/). The preregistered missingness_plan specified deterministic treatment of technical failures and required that such failures be logged and handled per analysis_plan; execution completed without technical failures affecting confirmatory pairs.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The experiment executed as preregistered and completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs. Execution manifest timestamps show the run started at 2026‑08‑29T23:01:17.772030+00:00 and completed at 2026‑08‑29T23:16:19.305763+00:00. Planned_episode_count = 400 (200 baseline + 200 guarded), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200 (execution/execution_manifest.json; execution/model_configuration.json).

Primary artifact‑grounded outcomes. The archived paired contingency counts are n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Marginal counts were baseline_success_count = 200 and guarded_success_count = 200 (analysis/condition_summary.csv), yielding success rates of 1.0 in both arms. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test produces p = 1.0 given zero discordant pairs. The preregistered bootstrap percentile CI for the absolute paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10000) is degenerate at [0.00, 0.00] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). These statistical outputs are arithmetic consequences of identical paired outcomes and are reported directly from the archived analysis artifacts.

Repair activity and candidate identity. Because generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate was used, each confirmatory pair shared the same initial LLM candidate file. Representative response files demonstrate identity between shared and per‑condition outputs (for example: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-baseline.txt, execution/responses/task-000001-guarded.txt). For every confirmatory pair the archived validator_trace records validation_after.valid == true, validation_after.violation_count == 0, and repair_applied == false (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json). Consequently, repair_attempts = 0/200 for the confirmatory cohort and the guarded arm had no opportunity to alter the shared candidate to create discordant outcomes.

Representative diagnostics. To illustrate task complexity despite the ceiling effect, six archived exemplar tasks (execution/representative_tasks/) summarize difficulty features: changed_interface_count = {1,2,2,2,2,2} (mean = 1.83), required_command_count = {4,2,6,4,3,6} (mean = 4.17), dependency_rule_count commonly = 2, and difficulty labels spanning medium/hard/very_hard. These diagnostics show that the confirmatory intents required nontrivial multi‑step sequences and dependency constraints even though the shared candidate satisfied the deterministic validator in every case.

Contamination and exclusions. The preregistered contamination checks flagged zero exact‑hash duplicates among confirmatory intents and recorded no high n‑gram overlap flags; no confirmatory episodes were excluded (analysis/contamination_summary.csv; execution/task_manifest.jsonl). The deterministic_reconciliation artifact confirms accounting consistency across episodes and conditions.

Interpretation of statistical vacuum. The degenerate bootstrap CI and McNemar p = 1.0 do not imply that verifiers are unnecessary in general; they are mathematical consequences of having no discordant pairs when the paired statistic depends solely on discordance. Under the preregistered shared‑candidate semantics the only path to discordance was an active repair that changed the shared candidate; because the shared candidate already passed, the repair step was never invoked and the confirmatory contrast could not reveal marginal repair utility.
sections.discussion:
Detectability tradeoff and formal power collapse. Paired designs control between‑intent variance by reducing across‑arm differences in starting material. Let S denote the event that the shared candidate passes the validator. When P(S) is close to 1 under the chosen generation semantics and model, the probability of observing any discordant pairs (n10 + n01 > 0) shrinks regardless of the conditional effectiveness of repairs on failing candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nontrivial baseline failure rate and a mass of discordant pairs driven by repair‑induced conversions; those assumptions failed for the observed shared candidate distribution, producing empirical power collapse. This formal explanation is supported by the archived contingency table and validator traces and explains why statistical inference was vacuous in the confirmatory run.

Design alternatives to restore detectability (artifact‑grounded recommendations). Based on the archived run parameters and artifacts, we identify concrete, artifact‑supported design changes that increase the opportunity for repairs to be exercised without requiring new experimental data in this paper: (A) independent per‑condition generation: produce separate LLM candidates for baseline and guarded arms (remove shared_initial_candidate) so that the guarded repair can act on independent failing candidates; (B) multiple independent draws per condition (k>1) with selection rules based on validator pass to expose diverse failure modes; (C) multi‑model or temperature sampling to increase candidate heterogeneity; (D) inclusion of adversarial or stress strata targeted at ordering and reachability constraints (label these strata as exploratory in preregistration); and (E) allow extended repair budgets when the repair prompt requires richer verifier counterexample context. Each recommended change directly addresses the detectability failure observed in the archived artifacts and can be implemented within the same orchestration framework.

Value of trace‑centered evaluation. The artifacts produced in this run show that trace‑level signals (repair_attempts, repair_prompt traces, Batfish counterexample provenance, violation_code taxonomy, and repair_applied flags) provide crucial process evidence distinct from final pass/fail outcomes. Even when final outcomes coincide, trace metrics can reveal near‑misses, partial repairs, or the absence of repair activity; our artifact bundle contains these traces (execution/scoring/*.json, execution/provider_calls/*) and supports reproducible secondary analyses focused on process evidence rather than binary endpoints.

Operational implications. For organizations adopting verifier‑in‑the‑loop deployments, the practical lesson is clear: if operational approval or auditability requires a single authoritative initial candidate, a verifier that only approves that candidate will rarely exercise repair logic. To realize repair gains in deployment, pipelines should either surface diverse candidate proposals, run adversarial perturbations as a canary before approval, or sample multi‑model candidates to increase the likelihood of encountering failing candidates that benefit from repair.

Threats to validity and limits of generalization. Internal validity: the principal internal limitation is the preregistered shared_initial_candidate choice combined with a single model family (gpt‑5‑mini), which restricted within‑study sensitivity. Construct validity: our deterministic validator implements a conservative pass rule (validation_after.valid==true and violation_count==0) that enforces parsing, task‑constraint, and Batfish reachability checks; different validator designs could change pass rates. External validity: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only; no proprietary vendor images were present. Conclusion validity: statistical inference collapsed because the required discordant information was absent. These threats and their artifact support are documented in the archived run (analysis/missingness_summary.csv; execution/model_configuration.json).
sections.conclusion: This preregistered, archived paired evaluation reveals an important experimental design lesson for NetOps researchers: generation semantics are a design lever that trades variance control for detectability of verifier utility. In our confirmatory cohort the shared initial candidate matched both baseline and guarded responses for all 200 pairs; no verifier repairs were applied (repair_attempts = 0/200) and the paired contingency reduced to n11 = 200, rendering McNemar/bootstrap inference vacuous (p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The artifact bundle substantiates these facts and enables reproducible diagnostics but does not permit broader generalization beyond the declared model, generation semantics, task generator, validator, and emulation choices. We recommend that future preregistered NetOps evaluations (1) explicitly assess detectability when selecting generation semantics, (2) include trace‑centered provenance metrics that reveal repair activity, and (3) adopt independent or multiple draws per condition (or multi‑model sampling) when the objective is to quantify marginal repair benefit. The archived artifacts provide a reproducible record for community inspection and for designing confirmatory NetOps experiments that avoid the ceiling effects documented here.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory). The study was executed autonomously from a frozen initial master prompt archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Declared LLM: gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) as recorded in execution/model_configuration.json. Orchestration/adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: CNSM2026_GVR_V1_001 was frozen before execution (preregistration manifest archived in the evidence bundle). Execution components: containerized Mininet‑style emulation using FRRouting and VyOS images; Batfish used as the formal verifier; deterministic task generator and the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scoring rule. The deterministic validator assigns verifier_pass when validation_after.valid == true and validation_after.violation_count == 0 in the archived validator_trace; this combines parsing/normalization, task‑constraint checks (required_sequence and preserve_unspecified_state), and Batfish reachability/policy tests (see execution/scoring/*.json for per‑task traces). The confirmatory run used a shared initial generation per intent for baseline and guarded conditions (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate), a preregistered design choice intended to control generation variance across paired units. All orchestration, model calls, verifications, emulation runs, scoring, logging, and analysis were performed autonomously per the preregistration; humans acted only as Research Director prior to the autonomy lock and to receive final outputs after autonomous completion. Execution completed without technical restarts affecting confirmatory pairs (completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). The artifact bundle includes archived raw responses, validator traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts (refer to execution/ and analysis/ paths in the bundle) for machine verification.
limitations: Single model family: only gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; conclusions do not generalize across models or families.
Device and vendor scope: emulation used FRRouting and VyOS images only (no proprietary vendor images).
Synthetic deterministic task generator: tasks were deterministically generated and may not capture full operator ambiguity, legacy runbook phrasing, or adversarial intent distributions.
Emulator fidelity: containerized Mininet‑style emulation does not fully replicate hardware idiosyncrasies, timing, or race conditions of production devices.

Design detectability tradeoff: shared_initial_generation was chosen to control generation variance but reduces sensitivity to detect marginal repair benefits (a principal internal‑validity limitation).
Ceiling effect: baseline single‑pass outputs passed the validator for all confirmatory intents, producing a null marginal effect and limiting exploratory inference.

Contamination uncertainty: deterministic exact‑hash checks found zero matches in confirmatory N and n‑gram overlap detectors reported no high‑overlap flags, but undetected paraphrase overlap with model training data cannot be fully ruled out.
Security scenarios: prompt‑injection, retrieval poisoning, and adversarial telemetry perturbations were not evaluated and remain open threats for agentic NetOps systems.
